routes.title: The Downtown Loop
routes.blurb: Roughly 1.7 miles, mostly flat with one climb back up from the lake. Budget 90–120 minutes at a casual pace, more if you linger at the waterfront.

steps.directions: Face south and start walking down Church Street Marketplace.
Continue south to the bottom of Church Street, where City Hall faces the park.
Head west one block on College Street to the library.
Backtrack toward Church Street and head north on Cherry Street toward Battery Park. The route goes slightly uphill, then down toward the bluff.
Walk south along Battery Street, back the way you came, taking in the historic houses.
Continue south and then down the hill toward the waterfront — via Pine Street or the Battery Street stairs/path — to Union Station.
Walk north along the waterfront bike path toward the old power plant.
Walk back south along the waterfront path, past Union Station, toward ECHO.
Walk out onto the bike path or the fishing pier just south of ECHO for the breakwater view.
Head back up College Street toward downtown, retracing part of your earlier route. This stretch is uphill.
Walk half a block to Nectar's.
Walk northwest back up to Church Street and climb to the top.

pins.title: The Unitarian Church
pins.tease: The white steeple everyone gives directions from, and its Revere bell
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street at the Pearl Street crossing, facing the white church across the street.
pins.script:
Look straight up the street. That white spire at the end of Church Street is the thing everything down here aims at. Two heavy brick buildings frame it: the Masonic Temple, finished in 1898, and the Richardson Building, 1895, put up to hold Burlington's largest department store. The state's own historic district file says the church provides a focal point for the area, and that directions in Burlington are frequently given in relation to it.

The building went up in 1816. The congregation had bought the land two years before that. Five acres of overgrown pasture on the northern edge of the village, for $1,000. The meeting house cost $22,185.34. The timbers came from the Browns River Valley. The brick was fired in Burlington. The nails were hammered by hand.

The architect was Peter Banner, working out of Boston. There is evidence that Charles Bulfinch supervised or amended Banner's plan. The tower rises about 170 feet.

Here is the part most people walk past. The bell in that tower was cast by Paul Revere's foundry, Revere and Sons, in October 1816. It weighed 1,286 pounds. Then somebody rang it too hard. In 1828 it cracked and had to be recast. In 1928 it was replaced outright with a bell from the Meneely foundry.

The church was dedicated on January 9, 1817. Its congregation calls it the oldest surviving place of worship in the city. It is the oldest remaining place of worship established by European settlers in Burlington.

You are standing at the top of the street. Everything else on this walk sits downhill from here. The marketplace. The park. The library. The bluff over the lake. In 1974 these three buildings around you were listed together on the National Register as the Head of Church Street Historic District.

pins.title: Church Street Marketplace
pins.tease: A Copenhagen street a student saw in 1962, rebuilt here
pins.stand_at: Stand mid-block on Church Street between Bank and Cherry, facing downhill toward City Hall.
pins.script:
Brick under your feet, no cars, benches down the middle. Behind you at the top of the slope, the white church spire. Ahead of you, downhill, City Hall.

Until 1980 this was a street. Traffic, curbs, parked cars, the whole thing.

The idea of closing it goes back to 1958, to a round of urban renewal discussions. It got its champion in 1962, when a Burlington architecture student named Bill Truex went to Copenhagen and saw the Stroget, a street the Marketplace's own history describes as a traffic-snarled nightmare that had been handed back to people on foot.

Burlington tested the idea before committing to it. A one-day street fair in 1971 drew about 15,000 people. A week-long fair the next year drew an estimated 50,000. That was the proof.

On July 7, 1980, the two blocks between College and Cherry closed to traffic for good. Sixteen months of construction followed, on a $6 million design by Carr, Lynch Associates with C.E. Maguire supervising the engineering, paid for with a federal grant and a city bond that Burlington voters passed. The Marketplace opened on September 15, 1981.

Now the part that surprises people who assume it arrived all at once. It didn't. On opening day, only two blocks of it existed. The top block, Cherry up to Pearl, the one you walked down to get here, was not closed and resurfaced in brick until 1994. And the block in front of City Hall, Main to College, was not finished until 2005.

So the four-block street with roughly 86 storefronts that everyone treats as one thing took 25 years to become one. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the American Planning Association named it one of America's Great Public Spaces. The stretch you would swear was always here, the block facing City Hall, has only been free of cars since 2005.

pins.title: City Hall Park
pins.tease: This lawn was voted into existence before the streets were drawn
pins.stand_at: Stand by the fountain in the middle of City Hall Park, facing the brick and marble front of City Hall.
pins.script:
Fountain in front of you. A ring of trees. And on the far side, brick and carved marble with a clock tower on top: City Hall.

This lawn is older than almost everything around it, and it was decided in a house three blocks downhill. In June 1798 the proprietors of Burlington held their last series of meetings at Gideon King Junior's house on King Street. At one of them, William Coit presented a final plan for the city, the grid that downtown streets still run on. And at those same meetings the proprietors voted to set aside the land you are standing on.

For its first century this was Court House Square. It sits deliberately partway between the waterfront and the commercial cluster up on College Hill, which may have been a compromise between two sets of business interests that each wanted the center of town nearer to them.

City Hall came much later. Burlington's 1850s city hall was badly built and falling apart. The replacement went to McKim, Mead and White of New York, with William M. Kendall as architect, and it opened to the public on May 12, 1928. It cost $475,000, which came in $25,000 under budget.

Look at what it is made of. The red brick, the carved marble, the granite, the slate on the roof. Nearly every finish material in that building was produced in Vermont. That was the point of it.

In 1983 the park and the buildings around it were listed on the National Register as the City Hall Park Historic District, eight acres bounded by Church, College, Main and St. Paul. Most of those buildings went up between about 1880 and 1930, replacing wooden ones.

The park itself had been reserved 185 years before that listing, by men who had not yet finished drawing the streets.

In addition they voted to set aside the land now known as City Hall Park.'

pins.title: Fletcher Free Library
pins.tease: A gift, a steel baron, and a ravine that nearly ate it
pins.stand_at: Stand on the College Street sidewalk in front of the library's stone steps, facing the columns.
pins.script:
Columns, stone steps, a Beaux-Arts front sitting right on College Street. This is the Fletcher Free Library, and Burlington has had a free library for more than 150 years.

It started with a gift. On July 14, 1873, Mrs. Mary L. Fletcher and her daughter, Miss Mary M. Fletcher, gave the city of Burlington $20,000 to found it. Half was to be spent on books. The other half started an endowment.

The library lived inside the old city hall building and outgrew it by 1901. That same year Andrew Carnegie gave $50,000 for a new building. A Burlington architect, Walter R. B. Willcox, won the competition to design it. It was dedicated and opened for business on August 17, 1904, the first of the four Carnegie libraries in Vermont.

Now the problem nobody planned for. There was a ravine on this site, and the ravine had been filled in. In 1973 the northwest corner of the foundation settled and the building took structural damage. The books had to leave. First to Contois Auditorium, then to the basement of Memorial Auditorium. Demolition was on the table.

What saved it was a committee with a very plain name: the Committee to Save the Fletcher Free Library Building. They got the building onto the National Register of Historic Places in August 1976. A federal Economic Development Administration grant of $234,000 paid for stabilization and exterior repairs in 1977.

Then Burlington voters approved a $2.4 million bond for an addition, and that addition was dedicated on January 4, 1981. It is the modern wing behind the old stone one, and it is the reason this is still a working library and not a plaque.

Historic preservation work on the 1904 Carnegie building itself began in 2025, paid for through Save America's Treasures and Vermont historic preservation grants.

pins.title: Little Italy
pins.tease: The ground you are standing on is what the bulldozers made
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of Cherry Street on the Battery Park Extension, by the green state historic marker, facing east up Cherry Street.
pins.script:
You are on a strip of grass at the foot of Cherry Street. The lake is below you to the west. The street climbs away from you to the east. There is a green state historic marker here. Read it if you want. Then look up Cherry Street, because that is where the neighborhood was.

Roughly six blocks, running east from Battery and Pearl to Pine Street, south to College, and back west to Battery. Houses, gardens, shops, families. The households were Italian American, and also French Canadian, Syrian, and other backgrounds. The interpretive signage puts it carefully. Many of the people, but not all the people, were the sons and daughters of Italian immigrants.

On May 17, 1966, a bulldozer crushed the walls of a tenement building on Cherry Street, then moved to the next building and did the same. Over the following two years, more than 160 buildings came down, housing 157 families, 67 individuals and 41 businesses. Twenty-seven acres cleared. It was called the Champlain Street Urban Renewal Project.

The last person out was Victoria Dutra, of 12 Cherry Street. Her home was demolished in 1968.

Here is the part that is easy to miss while you are standing on it. This ground is part of the project too. In 1966 the city acquired the buildings on the west side of Battery Street and took them down so that Battery Park could be extended south. The reason given at the time was to open up more of a lake view from the renewal area.

So the view you have right now was produced by the same clearance that removed the neighborhood behind you.

In 2011 the Vermont Division for Historic Preservation designated the former urban renewal neighborhood as Little Italy. The marker beside you was dedicated on October 8, 2011, forty-three years after the last house came down.

pins.title: Battery Park
pins.tease: The gun battery became a glass factory before it became a park
pins.stand_at: Stand at the western rim of Battery Park, at the railing above the bluff, facing the lake.
pins.script:
You are on the edge of a bluff. The lake is in front of you, the Adirondacks across it, and the ground drops away hard from your feet. That drop is why this is Battery Park.

During the War of 1812 the United States military put cannon up here to protect the harbor and stationed roughly 4,000 soldiers on and around this ground. Burlington sat within reach of the Canadian border, and the lake was the road an invasion would use. The park takes its name from the artillery, not from anything that happened afterward.

What you see now is about 14 acres. A bandshell, a playground, monuments. A bronze of the Civil War general William W. Wells. A red oak carving of Chief Grey Lock by the sculptor Peter Wolf Toth.

And here is the stretch of this place's history that almost nobody tells you.

Within about fifteen years of the soldiers leaving, this was heavy industry. In 1827 Doctor John Peck and Professor James Dean established the Champlain Glass Company on the former battery campsite. It is described as the first extensive manufacturing concern in the town. It covered about two acres. It employed about 100 people. It made window glass.

Frederick Smith, who arrived in Burlington the same year the works opened, ran the glassworks from 1834 until 1850, when the cost of fuel made it unprofitable and it shut down. Smith then subdivided the property himself and laid Park and Front Streets across the site.

So the order of things on this bluff is artillery, then a glass furnace, then a park. And the glass was not a small footnote to the neighborhood. It was the neighborhood. An 1839 survey labels the district that grew up around the works Glassville.

pins.title: Battery Street
pins.tease: The old waterline, and the shipyard that launched the world's second steamboat
pins.stand_at: Stand on the west sidewalk of Battery Street at College Street, facing the lake where the ground drops away.
pins.script:
Battery Street, with the ground falling away in front of you toward the rail line and the lake. Hold onto that drop, because it used to be the edge of the water.

This street was called Water Street. The lakeshore came right up to it. The shoreline is now hundreds of feet further out than it was. Everything between you and the water down there is made land, filled in across the 1800s for wharves, lumber yards and railroad track.

The state's historic survey calls this the Battery Street Historic District and describes it as Burlington's earliest settlement, an area of mixed commercial, light industrial and residential use developed from 1790 onward. It is on the National Register.

The man who ran the lake from here was Gideon King Junior. Between 1790 and 1812 he controlled lake traffic, working a route between Burlington, Saint Johns in Quebec, and Whitehall, New York. His house still stands at 35 King Street, a few blocks south of you, and the survey calls it one of Burlington's oldest structures.

And at the foot of King Street was Burlington's only shipyard. What came out of it was the steamboat Vermont, which the state survey calls the world's second commercial steamboat. John and James Winans built her here, and when they went to launch her in 1809 the engine was so heavy the hull stuck fast in the mud. They had to get her up onto logs and roll her into the lake.

Down at the foot of Maple Street, the old South Wharf, known as the Salt Dock, went in in 1810 to get cargo off the boats.

One more thing happened on this street. The second story of the Pomeroy House was a classroom for University of Vermont medical students from 1804 to 1822. The first regular lectures on anatomy and surgery ever given in Burlington were delivered in that house, to twelve students, in the winter of 1814.

pins.title: Union Station
pins.tease: The man who drew Grand Central drew this too
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway at the foot of Main Street, just east of the station, facing the clock in the stone above the entrance.
pins.script:
Look up at the clock set into the stone above the entrance. Around it, carved scrolls and swags of fruit and flowers tied with ribbons. And on top of the whole composition, an hourglass with wings.

This is Burlington Union Station. It opened in January 1916, and it was the city's second try. In 1867 the Vermont Central Railroad built a permanent station on fill at the foot of College Street. Four years later that railroad leased the Rutland Railroad, and the depot became a union station. Union means more than one railroad, sharing one building.

For the replacement, the city donated land and 15,000 dollars to build a new depot and reroute the tracks. The Central Vermont and the Rutland, who would jointly own it, put up the remaining 150,000 for a steel-framed neoclassical building in buff brick with cream limestone trim.

Here is the part people miss. The architect was Alfred Fellheimer. He had been involved with the design of Grand Central Terminal in Manhattan, and he already had extensive experience with railroad structures. The man who helped shape the biggest station in America also drew this one, at the bottom of Main Street.

Then the trains stopped. The Central Vermont ended passenger service in 1938. The Rutland ran passenger trains here until 1953, when a strike ended them. Two years after that, Green Mountain Power converted the station into office space. The building stayed. The trains did not. Main Street Landing owns it now, and it holds businesses and organizations.

Walk around to the lake side and you will find a platform and a canopy. The Vermont Agency of Transportation built them, with site preparation done in 2020 and 2021.

On July 29, 2022, Amtrak began direct service to Burlington when the Ethan Allen Express was extended north from Rutland.

Sixty-nine years separated the last Rutland passenger train from the first Amtrak train to pull in behind this building.

pins.title: The FRAME
pins.tease: They fixed the power plant by taking most of it away
pins.stand_at: Stand on the path just east of the red steel structure, facing it with the lake behind it.
pins.script:
In front of you is a red steel skeleton with the sky showing through it. No roof. Almost no walls. That is not decay. That is the design.

This was the Moran plant, Burlington's own municipal generating station. Construction started in 1952. It opened two years later, in 1954, as a 30-megawatt coal-fired power plant, right here on the waterfront.

In 1977 it did something unusual. The plant made its first experimental conversion from coal to wood chips. A second unit was converted successfully in 1979. Vermont trees, chipped and hauled in, turned into electricity on the shore of Lake Champlain.

The plant was decommissioned in 1986. Then it sat. For more than three decades a brick shell occupied some of the most valuable open ground in the city, and nobody could agree what it should become. On March 4, 2008, Burlington voters approved a 21 million dollar renovation plan for it. That plan was never built.

Here is the surprise. The idea that finally worked was to take most of the building away.

In August 2020 the city broke ground. Crews peeled back the brick exterior, kept the steel superstructure underneath, and left it standing open to the weather. Not restored. Not replaced. Reduced to its bones, and then painted a striking red.

The ribbon was cut on November 15, 2022, on about six million dollars of work. The head of Burlington City Arts said the day marked the transition of the space from the unsustainable energy of coal to the cleanest, most renewable energy there is, which is creativity.

Look into the northwest bay. Two custom swinging benches hang there, designed and manufactured with Generator, a Burlington maker space. The group that raised money for them pulled in over 22,000 dollars in five weeks of crowdfunding, matched with 40,000 from the state's Better Places program.

There is now free public wifi, seasonal restrooms, and a community idea board inside the rib cage of a coal plant.

pins.title: ECHO
pins.tease: Eighty-four million gallons of fuel used to sit here
pins.stand_at: Stand on the plaza at the foot of College Street, outside ECHO's main entrance, with the building on your left and the lake beyond it.
pins.script:
In front of you is ECHO, the lake aquarium and science center at the foot of College Street. Behind it, open water. Now put fuel tanks on this ground.

By 1958 there were 83 fuel tanks on the Burlington waterfront, holding a total of 84 million gallons. This was not a park. It was a tank farm with rail yards, and the railroad held the filled land it stood on.

In 1975 the city passed an ordinance that gave the oil companies twenty years to vacate the property. In 1986 the bike path along the water was completed with state and federal money. But the decisive fight happened in court.

In 1989 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled, in State versus Central Vermont Railway, that the filled land here was impressed by the public trust doctrine. Industrial uses that no longer benefited the public, storage tanks included, had to go. The court left a list of what the waterfront could be instead: parks and open space, recreation, marinas open to the public on a nondiscriminatory basis, water-dependent uses, boating and related services.

Here is the surprise. The ground you are standing on is largely not natural shoreline. It is fill, dumped to make room for the railroad. And it was that artificial origin, land made out of a public lake, that gave the city its legal claim to take it back.

The city acquired 60 acres of the waterfront from the railway. In 1991 the Legislature granted Burlington permission to develop the area by the Coast Guard station at College Street into a park.

ECHO itself was dedicated on May 31, 2003. The name stands for ecology, culture, history, and opportunities for stewardship. It succeeded the Lake Champlain Basin Science Center, and it carries the name of Senator Patrick Leahy, who secured the federal funding for it.

Inside are more than 70 species of live animals: fish, amphibians, invertebrates, reptiles.

The building that went up where the tanks came down was Vermont's first LEED-certified green building.

pins.title: The Breakwater
pins.tease: In 1876 this wall of stone caught five people out of a gale
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway beside the Burlington Community Boathouse, at the railing, facing straight out at the low stone line offshore.
pins.script:
Look straight out at the water. That long low line of stone running parallel to the shore is the Burlington Breakwater. It is not a reef. It is a nineteenth-century engineering project, and it is still doing the job it was built for.

Work began in 1837. The first section was V-shaped and a thousand feet long, completed in 1854 at a cost of 28,727 dollars. In 1867 the breakwater was extended 1,500 feet to the north. A final 360-foot section was finished in 1890. The main run measures 3,793 feet.

Underneath the waterline it is timber. Log cribs, joined by notched corners, most of them laid on a rubble foundation and packed with rubblestone. Hemlock in the lower levels, white pine in the upper. Most of the upper cribbing has rotted and been replaced with stone since, and the lake-facing side was faced in riprap in 1961. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on June 6, 2003, as a rare example of a nineteenth-century timber-cribbed stone breakwater.

Wooden lighthouses were first placed on the ends in 1857. The northern tower burned in 1870. The southern light was knocked over in a storm in 1876.

That same year, this wall of stone saved five lives.

On December 9, 1876, a powerful winter gale caught the sailing canal boat General Butler as she came up the lake. Her steering mechanism broke. Her captain, William Montgomery of Isle La Motte, rigged a tiller bar to the steering post and tried to work around the breakwater. He did not make it. The Butler crashed headlong into the stone, and one by one every person aboard jumped onto the breakwater as she went down.

Then they were stranded on a rock wall in a December gale. A Burlington ship chandler named James Wakefield and his son rowed out in a 14-foot lighthouse boat and took all five to safety.

The General Butler is still out there. She rests in 40 feet of water, about 75 yards west of the southern end of the breakwater, a Vermont underwater historic preserve.

pins.title: Memorial Auditorium
pins.tease: This building exists because voters refused a smaller one
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Main Street sidewalk below the auditorium, near the corner of South Union Street, facing the front steps.
pins.script:
The big building above you on the corner of Main and South Union has been locked since 2016. Memorial Auditorium. Look at the scale of it. This was built to hold thousands of people at once.

It exists because Burlington citizens refused something smaller.

In 1925 the editor-in-chief of the Burlington Free Press called for a large, separate memorial auditorium with tablets on the walls of the main lobby, rather than a smaller memorial hall folded into the new city hall then being planned for Church Street. In January 1926 the mayor's office presented city hall plans with a 1,000-seat auditorium inside. Many citizens complained. They wanted a completely separate building, at another location, and bigger.

The city gave way. In February 1926 a new city hall design appeared without an auditorium, by the firm of McKim, Mead and White. That is the building on Church Street. And a separate memorial auditorium with a capacity of 4,000 was announced for this corner, to go to the voters.

In March 1926 they approved it. The architect was Frank L. Austin of Burlington, who also designed the Central Fire Station and the junior high school. Ground was broken within a month.

Then the money ran out. Twice. Work stalled in December 1926 until voters authorized more. By April 1927 they approved another 100,000 dollar bond. The original plan had been that the auditorium would cost no more than 150,000 dollars, funded from the remaining balance of a 750,000 dollar bond. The final figure, with heating, lighting and all fixtures, was 233,185 dollars.

It opened on March 28, 1928, to a crowd of three thousand. The Burlington Symphony Orchestra played the first concert here on April 15, to 1,700 people. The 1929 Burlington Automobile Show was advertised as the largest show north of Boston. Simon and Garfunkel played this room on March 12, 1967.

It was listed on the National Register on October 13, 1988. It was closed in December 2016 on the recommendation of the City Engineer.

pins.title: Nectar's
pins.tease: A Greek immigrant let an unknown band flail here for two years
pins.stand_at: Stand on the north sidewalk of Main Street outside 188 Main Street, facing the storefront and its sign.
pins.script:
You are outside 188 Main Street. A brick building with a neon sign. For fifty years this was Nectar's.

Nectar Rorris came to the United States from Greece in 1956. He borrowed money from family, the way he said everyone did, and in 1975 he opened a restaurant and bar here. It sold gravy fries. French fries under gravy. That stayed on the menu for the rest of the room's life.

In the early 1980s a young Burlington band got a residency in this room that ran close to two years. They were still working out what they were. Rorris let them do it in public, night after night, in front of people eating gravy fries.

The band was Phish.

Here is the surprise. Rorris never expected any of it. He said he never imagined the Vermont restaurant and music club he opened would become synonymous with a jam band. He credited Phish with giving Nectar's a national spotlight, and with making it a place that local and traveling musicians sought out. Phish credited him right back, for giving them a stage to experiment on when they were starting out. In 1992 they named an album A Picture of Nectar, after the man and after this bar.

Then Main Street got torn up. Construction cut the foot traffic. Costs climbed. In May 2025 Nectar's announced it would close for the summer and blamed the construction. The pause was supposed to be temporary.

On July 30, 2025, the owners said it was permanent. Lease negotiations with the building's owner, Joe Handy, had not worked out.

A former employee, counting what went with it, listed a music venue, and employment for a lot of chefs, a lot of sound engineers, a lot of bartenders, a lot of servers. He said that until the rest of Main Street is finished, he does not see a way this makes sense.

Fifty years of a Burlington bar ended over a lease and a street that was dug up.

pins.title: The First Ben & Jerry's
pins.tease: An ice cream empire started in a gas station right here
pins.stand_at: Stand on the southwest corner of College and St. Paul streets and look down at the sidewalk for a brass plaque.
pins.script:
Look down at the sidewalk. Somewhere near your feet on this corner there is a brass plaque set into the concrete. It marks a gas station that is no longer here.

On May 5, 1978, two friends opened an ice cream shop in a renovated gas station on this corner, College and St. Paul. They had taken a correspondence course in ice cream making from the creamery at Pennsylvania State University. They had about twelve thousand dollars. Their names were Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield.

That is the whole origin of Ben and Jerry's. Not a factory. Not Waterbury. A repurposed filling station at a downtown intersection, opening in May, in a state where the ice cream season is short and the first winter is the real test.

They got through the winter. And in those early years they did something with the building that would be hard to arrange now. They hung a big white sheet against the brick wall beside the shop and projected movies onto it, and people stood around outside with cones and watched.

For one of the free cone days they staged a bit out front. Jerry would come out and announce a rare visit from a mystic of the east. Then Ben would appear, barefoot, wrapped in white sheets, wearing a turban, to the sound of Rubberband Man by the Spinners. He would lie down on a wooden bench and bare his stomach. Jerry would balance a cinder block on it and bring down a sledgehammer.

The shop is gone. The building was torn down. What is here now is a surface parking lot, which is about the least romantic possible ending for the birthplace of Ben and Jerry's.

The plaque came in 1988, for the company's tenth anniversary. They pressed it into the sidewalk at this corner and printed thousands of T-shirts that read: BE 10 AGAIN.

It is the only thing left on the site.

pins.title: The Mall Block
pins.tease: Burlington tore down a mall and then stared at the hole
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street at the Cherry Street corner and look west, into the block behind the storefronts.
pins.script:
Look west into this block. Within living memory it has been an enclosed shopping mall, an open hole in the ground, and a construction site.

The mall came first. It opened in 1976 as the Burlington Square Mall, anchored by a department store called Porteous. An indoor mall, dropped into the middle of a downtown that already had a pedestrian shopping street. Later it was renamed the Burlington Town Center. Filene's, later Macy's, arrived in 1999. L.L. Bean came in 2014.

In December of 2013 an investor group bought the property for twenty-five million dollars, and in November of 2014 announced a two hundred million dollar plan to knock it down and build something much bigger. Demolition began in December 2017. Then the work stopped.

For four years the middle of downtown Burlington was an open excavation. People called it the pit. Not affectionately. The last businesses in the surviving stub of the mall shut for good in early 2022.

Construction restarted in 2022, under local developers. In September of 2025 the first building opened: a hundred and sixty-one room hotel, fifty-three apartments, ground floor retail, a restaurant and a cafe. Studios listed around sixteen hundred and fifty dollars a month. The two bedroom penthouse listed at sixty-eight hundred.

And the project got a new name, which is the part worth noticing. Burlington Square Mall became Burlington Town Center, became CityPlace Burlington, and is now called Burlington Square. After fifty years and one very long hole, the block is back to almost exactly the name it started with.

The second building, roughly three hundred and twenty more apartments and another hotel, is still going up. Seventy-three of the units are meant to be affordable. As of the spring of 2026 none of them had been built, and the deadline had been pushed to the end of 2027.

pins.title: The Boathouse
pins.tease: The building you are looking at is floating
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of College Street where the pavement meets the boathouse's landward end.
pins.script:
The boathouse in front of you is floating.

It is not on pilings and it is not on fill. In May of 1988 crews floated an old barge into place at the base of College Street and built the boathouse on top of it. Work started on May 21. It opened to the public shortly before the Fourth of July that same summer.

That is fast, and it was the point. Burlington was trying to turn an industrial shoreline into a public one, and the boathouse was the first thing built here that people could walk into. The bike path was finished around the same time.

The design is a copy of something that used to stand on this exact water.

The Lake Champlain Yacht Club was founded on this working waterfront in 1887. There was no land to be had, so in 1888 the club built its first two-story clubhouse out over the water, on pilings.

It burned in 1901.

They built another one. That one burned in 1911.

They built a third. In 1936 it was declared unsafe and too expensive for the club to fix, so they sold it to the ferry company, which turned it into a ferry station. The club gave up on Burlington, bought property in Shelburne in the early 1960s, and put up a modest new clubhouse there in 1963.

Then the city went looking for a design for a public boathouse. The architect who won it, Marcel Beaudin, was a yacht club member. He drew the new building to echo the old clubhouses, and when he made his pitch he included a photograph of the 1888 clubhouse so officials could see the link.

The barge you are looking at floats on the spot where those pilings stood.

pins.title: The Firehouse
pins.tease: That tower was built to hang wet hoses in
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Church Street Marketplace bricks directly in front of 135 Church Street, looking up at the brick tower.
pins.script:
Look up. The brick tower above you is 85 feet tall, and it was not built for the bell.

It was built to hang fire hoses in, so they could dry. That is the whole reason it is that shape: a narrow shaft tall enough to hold a length of wet hose hanging straight down.

This is the Ethan Allen Firehouse, 135 Church Street, designed by the local architect A. B. Fisher and completed in 1889. The style is a commercial variation of Richardsonian Romanesque.

It was home to the Ethan Allen Engine Company Number Four, one of seven volunteer fire companies in Burlington. And a volunteer engine house was more than an emergency service. It was where the members socialized, broke bread, and shared ideas. A private club that also happened to put out your fire.

The company started with horse-drawn equipment. Later it was folded into the city's fire department, and the building was adapted to house motorized fire equipment. After that the Burlington Police Department moved in, and stayed until the late 1960s.

It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 16, 1971.

Here is the surprise. The bell that belongs in that tower spent decades somewhere else. It ended up in the collection of the Shelburne Museum, down the road, an artifact of a building still standing on Church Street.

Then it came back. On September 12, 2002, the original bell was hoisted back into the firehouse tower, where it had hung when the building was new.

Burlington City Arts had already moved a gallery into half of the ground floor in 1995. In 2002 the whole building opened to the public as the Firehouse Center for the Visual Arts. It is now the BCA Center: contemporary art exhibitions in a nineteenth-century engine house, under a tower designed to dry hose.

pins.title: The Follett House
pins.tease: The columns face the lake because the money came off the lake
pins.stand_at: Stand on the College Street sidewalk opposite the white-columned brick mansion, just uphill from Battery Street.
pins.script:
Six fluted Doric columns, a pediment, and a front that does not face the street. The house is turned west, toward the lake. That was deliberate. The money that built it came off the water.

Timothy Follett was a shipping man on Lake Champlain, and at the peak of his fortune he built a house to prove it. He put it up in 1840 and hired Ammi B. Young to design it. Young is the architect of Vermont's second State House, in Montpelier. What he built here is brick, two and a half stories, clapboarded, on a stone foundation, five bays across, with a balcony running the full width of the second floor.

Then Follett changed businesses. In 1845 he became the first president of the Burlington and Rutland Railroad. Railroads were the future, and the future ruined him. The line failed, Follett lost his fortune in the 1850s, and he lost the house with it. He died in 1857.

The building kept going without him. A square cupola went on in the 1880s. Institutions moved through it, including at one point the local Veterans of Foreign Wars chapter. Since 1885 it has held institutional tenants rather than a family. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

Then the near miss. The Pomerleau real estate agency acquired the property in 1978 to restore it, and a damaging fire hit at the very start of the project. The restoration was finished anyway. The house has been offices since.

Look down College Street toward the water and try to picture the ridge above the harbor lined with houses like this one, built by men who owned boats. This is the last of Burlington's grand nineteenth-century lakeside mansions.

pins.title: The Howard Opera House
pins.tease: There was a fourteen-hundred-seat theater above these shop windows
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street just south of Bank, in front of the long brick block on the west corner, and look up above the shop windows.
pins.script:
You are standing under a theater. Look above the shop windows on this corner. Brick, a hundred and thirty feet along Church Street, seventy-six feet along Bank, sixty feet tall. Behind that wall, on the upper floors, there used to be an auditorium with enough chairs for between thirteen hundred and fourteen hundred people.

John Purple Howard paid for it. Burlington born, he went to New York as a young man and made a fortune in the hotel business. In 1877, when word got around that he was putting up a business block on this corner, townspeople started lobbying him to include a hall. The theater in City Hall was too small, they said, unsafe, and an acoustical outrage.

He agreed. He hired Stephen Hatch, another Vermonter who had gone to New York, and told him the building should be as good as anybody's. He was prepared to spend about a hundred thousand dollars.

It opened on the evening of February 24, 1879, with a touring company singing Lucia di Lammermoor. Gas fixtures lit the walls, and gas jets hidden inside the dome made heat, which pulled the air upward and ventilated the room.

Electric light arrived in October of 1886. And the manager used it only in the foyer, and in the auditorium between the acts. Touring companies wanted the gas kept burning during the show. Gaslight was warm, and it threw softer shadows on an actor's face.

On November 14, 1881, Howard gave the entire block away. Stores, theater, hall and weather station, all of it, to the Home for Destitute Children. The deed said the block could not be sold and the theater could not close before November of 1901.

The merchants downstairs eventually bought out the theater lease. Their fire insurance was brutal, because of all that flammable space over their heads.

The last performance was November 30, 1904.

pins.title: The Bike Path
pins.tease: Follow this pavement north and it runs out into the lake
pins.stand_at: Stand on the paved path at the north end of Waterfront Park, facing north along the shore.
pins.script:
The pavement under you is a railroad bed. The Rutland Railroad built the Island Line here in 1901 and ran it north out of Burlington, along this shore, and then straight out into open water.

To reach the Champlain Islands the railroad did not build a bridge. It built a causeway. Crews tipped marble blocks into the lake for three and a half miles, from Colchester Point across to South Hero, and laid track on top of the rubble. It is still out there. You can walk on it.

Passenger service on the Island Line ended after an employee strike in late June of 1953. The final trains ran on September 25, 1961. In 1963 the state of Vermont bought the abandoned lines.

The path came later, and it came from a vote. In 1981 Burlington voters approved a bike path on the old right of way with seventy-five percent support. It was fully funded by 1984, and by 1986 the waterfront stretch was complete. In 2010 the trail was inducted into the Rails-to-Trails Hall of Fame.

Here is the part people do not expect. The causeway has a hole in it. About two hundred feet of open water, called the Cut, where a swing bridge used to pivot aside to let boats through. The bridge is gone. The gap is not.

Since 1998 a ferry has crossed it. Not a car ferry. A bike ferry, run by the nonprofit Local Motion. It carries bicycles, trailers, wheelchairs and other mobility devices, and it takes anyone who bikes, walks or rolls out to it. No motor vehicles.

From here it is about eight paved miles to the end of the pavement, and five more of crushed gravel out on the marble.

pins.title: The King Street Ferry Dock
pins.tease: The dock is still here. The ferry is not.
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of King Street beside the ferry terminal building, facing out at the water.
pins.script:
There is a ferry terminal beside you. Look at the water. There is no ferry.

Lake Champlain Transportation says it has been carrying people across this lake since 1826. Two hundred years. The company still runs two crossings, and both of them are somewhere else. Grand Isle to Plattsburgh runs around the clock, all year, breaking ice when it has to, and takes about twelve minutes. Charlotte to Essex runs year round as well, weather permitting.

The Burlington boat went to Port Kent, New York, and it was the long one. It crossed the maximum width of Lake Champlain. It took about an hour. It never ran in winter. It was less a commute than a passage, and people used it that way.

It last operated in 2019. It has not run since.

In June of 2022 the company said the line was postponed for the near future. Staffing was tight. The pandemic had wrecked the economics. By then the loading apparatus had already been pulled off this terminal, maintenance work had been moved north to Grand Isle, and the company was talking about putting a restaurant on the site instead.

On the New York side, a town supervisor said the loss had cut into tourism and forced residents to drive to other ferry terminals. Nothing has been announced since.

So this is a dock with no crossing. The building is here. The pilings are here. The schedule is not. The water in front of you is the widest part of the lake, and on a clear day the far shore is the place the boat used to land.

About one million passengers cross Lake Champlain by ferry every year. Not one of them from this dock.

pins.title: Main Street Landing
pins.tease: Two women got this land after a hundred million dollar plan died
pins.stand_at: Stand at the corner of College and Lake streets, outside the brick and stone building whose four sides do not match.
pins.script:
Stand at this corner and walk your eyes around the building. Each face of it is different. Different materials, different rhythm, as though four separate buildings had grown together.

That was the instruction. The owners told their architect they wanted every facade to look like a different building, built out of local brick and stone, feeling like the pioneer shops of the eighteen hundreds. He came back with the drawing in two weeks.

Now the part that is hard to believe. In the mid nineteen eighties this corner was inside a twenty-seven acre, hundred million dollar development called the Alden Waterfront Project. Hundreds of condominiums. Offices. A seven story hotel. A large parking garage. An art museum. An ice rink. Bernie Sanders, mayor at the time, backed it. The city council backed it. In December of 1985 the bond vote that would have paid for the public pieces failed, and the whole thing collapsed.

Two women were left standing in the wreckage. Melinda Moulton had been the project's director of operations. Lisa Steele came out of a divorce owning the waterfront land. Steele phoned Moulton to help her sell it off. Moulton proposed they build it themselves instead. That company is Main Street Landing.

Here is the number that tells the story. Under the Alden plan, eleven acres had been optioned from the railroad at five hundred thousand dollars an acre. After the plan died, the city sued the railroad under the public trust doctrine, and got waterfront land for sixty-five thousand dollars an acre.

Their first two buildings opened in 1995. This one, the Lake and College building, opened on July 3, 2005. A hundred and twenty thousand square feet, with a two hundred and twenty seat performing arts center inside it, and Silver LEED certification.

In February of that year it had no tenants at all. The anchor signed after touring an unfinished top floor at ten below zero, with plastic sheeting flapping over the window openings. That tenant was Seventh Generation, and it took thirty-six thousand square feet.

pins.title: The Masonic Temple
pins.tease: Vermont's Masons built a castle at the top of Church Street
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street just below Pearl, on the west side, facing the gray stone building with the steep pyramid roof.
pins.script:
Look up. Five stories of rough gray stone, and a slate roof that climbs to a pyramid over the corner. This is the Masonic Temple, at the head of Church Street, where Church meets Pearl.

It went up in 1897 and 1898. Not as a store. Not as an office block. It was built to be the state headquarters of the Grand Lodge of Vermont, Free and Accepted Masons.

The Masons had wanted this for a long time. The Grand Lodge picked Burlington as the site back in 1868. Thirty years went by before the building existed. When it was done it had cost 87,500 dollars.

They hired John McArthur Harris, of the Philadelphia firm Wilson Brothers and Company. He gave them Richardsonian Romanesque. Heavy masonry. Round arches. A roof with real weight to it. Step around to the Pearl Street side and look at the windows there. They climb the wall at an angle. That is a staircase, showing through the stone.

The lodge rooms were upstairs. The ground floor was rented out to shops and offices from the start. A temple with storefronts under it, because the storefronts were supposed to pay for the temple.

That is not how it went. The Masons were already talking about selling the building in 1914, sixteen years after they finished it. A fire in 1933 did about sixty thousand dollars of damage. Membership thinned through the rest of the century. In 1984 a group called the One Church Street Partnership bought the building and renovated it.

Now every floor is retail and offices. No lodge meets here. The last Burlington lodge merged away in 2016 and moved out to Williston.

The building is protected all the same. It is one of three in the Head of Church Street Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 15, 1974. The other two are the brick meetinghouse above you and the turreted building across the street.

pins.title: Perkins Pier
pins.tease: This quiet pier was once stacked forty feet high
pins.stand_at: Stand out near the end of Perkins Pier, at the rail, facing north up the shoreline.
pins.script:
You are standing on made land. The lake used to reach further in than this. In 1810 a man named Curtis Holgate built a wharf at the bottom of Maple Street and filled part of the lake to hold it up. That is the ground under your shoes.

For a while this was the steamboat landing. Canal and stagecoach traffic was routed here by 1823, and the wharf sat at the center of one of the busiest commercial districts in town. Freight moved off boats and onto wagons right where you are standing.

Then came the wood. Look north along the shoreline and take the boats away. Fill it with lumber. Boards stacked thirty to forty feet high, covering more than thirty acres of waterfront.

In 1865 Burlington was the third most important and largest lumber port in the United States. Some accounts put it second. Only Chicago and Albany moved more. Vermont's own forests were largely cut over by then, so the lumber came south from Canada by boat, got sorted and resawn here, and left by rail.

The numbers kept climbing. In 1873 this harbor handled upwards of 123 million feet of lumber in a year. At the peak, in 1889, shipments topped 375 million feet. At least twelve wharves worked the harbor.

Then it stopped. New tariffs in the early 1890s cut off the Canadian supply. By 1926 the harbor took in about thirty boats of lumber a year.

The waterfront did not go quiet, though. It went flammable. Oil companies took the empty wharves and built tanks. By 1958 there were eighty-three fuel tanks along this shore, holding eighty-four million gallons.

Perkins Pier was founded the next year, in 1959.

pins.title: The Maltex Building
pins.tease: Maypo was invented inside this building
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Pine Street sidewalk in front of the four-story brick building with the tall windows.
pins.script:
Four stories of brick, tall windows, and a name across the top. Maltex. This was a cereal factory.

William J. Van Patten, a Burlington druggist and politician, founded the Malted Cereal Company in 1899 and had this building put up on Pine Street in 1900. The product was a hot cereal made from wheat and barley. It was called Maltex. The recipe outlived the factory. A company in Ohio makes it now.

Here is the part worth knowing. In 1950 the company invented Maypo, a hot oat cereal flavored with maple. That happened here, on this block.

The end came without warning. On May 9, 1969, the vice president of the company came in from Missouri and told the workers the factory was closing that day. Production left Vermont.

The building sat. In 1983 a man named Rick Davis bought it and cut it into space for small businesses, which is still what it is. That move, repeated up and down this street, is how a corridor of dead factories became an arts district. The South End Art Hop runs its thirty-fourth year in September of 2026, free, across more than a hundred locations along a two-mile stretch of this street.

Now stop looking at the buildings and think about the ground.

A few blocks south of here is the Pine Street Barge Canal. It is a federal Superfund site. Thirty-eight acres: a canal, a turning basin, wetlands, and a pond.

A plant on Pine Street used to make the city's gas by cooking coal. It ran until 1966. The waste went into the wetland. In the 1960s and 1970s an oil-like material began seeping out of the ground into the canal and the basin, and Burlington drinks from Lake Champlain. The Environmental Protection Agency settled on a remedy in 1998 and finished the work in 2004, capping the contaminated sediment underwater instead of digging it out.

The pond the coal tar seeped into had a name. It was called Maltex Pond.

pins.title: Richardson Place
pins.tease: The turrets say Richardson but everyone here says Abernethy's
pins.stand_at: Stand on the east sidewalk of Church Street about halfway between Pearl and Cherry, looking back up the hill at the brick building with the round turrets.
pins.script:
Up the hill from you, on the east side of Church Street, there is a castle. Brick, with round bays that bulge out from the corners and finish in cone-shaped roofs, and dormers punched into a steep roofline.

The style is called Chateauesque. Chateau, French for castle. It is one of very few buildings in Burlington that use it.

This is 2 Church Street, built in 1895, and it did not go up as a shop. It went up as a department store, the largest in Burlington, planted at the top of the hill where Church Street starts.

That siting was not an accident of the market. Church Street runs four blocks, from Pearl at the top down to Main at the bottom. From almost anywhere on it, if you look uphill, those cones are what closes the view.

It is one of three buildings in the Head of Church Street Historic District, all added to the National Register of Historic Places together in July of 1974. A church, a Masonic lodge and a store, at one intersection.

Now look at the small balconies on the front. There is a letter worked into the ironwork. An R. That is the Richardson in Richardson Place, put on the building the year it opened, and it is still up there.

Here is the thing. Almost nobody who grew up in Burlington calls this the Richardson Building. They call it Abernethy's. Abernethy's Department Store filled these floors for decades, selling high-end clothing and accessories for men and women, and it stayed until the 1980s. Ask anybody on this street over sixty what building you are looking at, and Abernethy's is the answer you will get.

The R is still on the railing. The name people actually use belongs to somebody else.

pins.title: St. Paul's Cathedral
pins.tease: The church burned and the city traded it a lake view
pins.stand_at: Stand in the plaza on the Cherry Street side of the concrete cathedral, near the tall bell tower, facing the lake.
pins.script:
In front of you is a wall of raw concrete. Poured in place, left rough, nothing faced over it. This is the Cathedral Church of St. Paul, and that tall element beside the sanctuary is a bell tower.

Go closer to it. The bells inside are older than everything around them. There are eight of them, cast in 1895 by the Meneely bell foundry in Troy, New York. They spent their first seventy-six years hanging in a completely different building.

That building was a Gothic Revival stone church, dedicated in 1832, and it stood on Bank Street between St. Paul and Pine, a few blocks east of here and up the hill. The parish had organized in 1830. Its first service was held in the old courthouse on June 12, 1831. The church was enlarged three times, in 1851, in 1866, and in 1910. In 1965 the diocese made it the cathedral of Vermont.

On February 15, 1971, it burned.

What happened next only happens in a city in the middle of urban renewal. The parish's block, occupied for almost a hundred and forty years, was useful to the city's redevelopment plans. So the city offered a trade. Land down here, on the edge of the bluff, looking west at Lake Champlain and the Adirondacks.

They took it. An international design competition went to Thomas Cullins and William Henderson of Burlington Associates. The new cathedral was consecrated on November 11, 1973, two and a half years after the fire.

Inside it is concrete, white oak, acoustic panelling and slate, with a glass wall aimed at the water. Outside it is Brutalism, and the concrete is doing exactly what the style asks for: it shows you how the building was made.

The building is 1973. The bells in its tower were cast in 1895.

pins.title: The Flynn
pins.tease: Vermont opened a half-million-dollar palace into the Depression
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Main Street sidewalk outside 153 Main Street, facing the marquee.
pins.script:
You are looking at the marquee of the Flynn, 153 Main Street. Flat facade, big lit sign, the whole thing pushed right up to the sidewalk.

On the night of Wednesday, November 26, 1930, floodlights danced above Burlington to herald what was billed as Vermont's newest and largest entertainment palace. It cost 500,000 dollars. It was the idea of a local entrepreneur named John J. Flynn and his investors in the Queen City Realty Company, and it was designed as a state-of-the-art facility for both touring stars of vaudeville and motion pictures.

Sit with that date for a second. November 1930. The stock market had crashed thirteen months earlier. Burlington opened a half-million-dollar Art Deco theater into the first full winter of the Great Depression.

Here is the surprise. The building was designed for live vaudeville, and the first thing that ever ran on that stage was a movie. A comedy called Big Money.

The architects were William Luther Mowll and Roger Glade Rand. What they delivered was not just a hall. Flynn and his backers called it an entertainment complex, a state-of-the-art facility built to hold two kinds of show at once.

There was an organ, too. A Wurlitzer built in 1925, opus 1200, Style H. It started life at Burlington's Majestic Theatre, moved here, and eventually left for a local convent.

Then multiplexes arrived in the 1970s and the theater declined. In 1981 the Lyric Theatre company rediscovered the building, and restoration of the Art Deco theater began that year. A second wave of work in the late 1990s and early 2000s took the interior back toward its original look and added FlynnSpace, a smaller performance venue downstairs.

It stopped being a movie house. It runs on live performance now, as the Flynn Center for the Performing Arts.

The Flynn was recognized by the Art Deco Societies of America as one of the country's ten most important Art Deco restoration projects.

pins.title: The UVM Green
pins.tease: Lafayette laid a stone here. It is not where he left it.
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway in the middle of the University Green, facing east toward the long building with the tower.
pins.script:
You are standing on a rectangle of grass that a university was built around. Look east at the long building with the tower. That is Old Mill. It is not one building.

The University of Vermont was chartered in 1791, the same year Vermont became the fourteenth state. It was the fifth college in New England, after Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth and Brown. Ira Allen led the drive to charter it and to put it here, on the hill above Burlington Bay. The bronze Ira Allen on this green is much newer. James Wilbur donated it to the university in 1921.

The first college building went up on this spot in 1801 and 1802. On May 28, 1824, it burned to the ground. A student had been feeding wood shavings into a stove. The draft carried the glowing shavings up a brick chimney and dropped them back down onto a corner of the roof.

Burlington paid to rebuild. In August of 1824 a citizens' committee announced it had raised $8,362.

Now the part that surprises people. They did not put up one building. They put up two, three stories each, set seven or eight feet apart on purpose so a fire could not jump between them. Governor Cornelius Van Ness laid the cornerstone of North College on April 26, 1825.

Two months later Burlington got a celebrity. The Marquis de Lafayette was thirteen months into a tour of all twenty-four states. On the evening of June 29, 1825, he laid the cornerstone of South College with Masonic rites, anointing it with oil, wine and corn. Then he went to dinner at Grasse Mount and left that night by steamboat.

A third building, Middle College, filled the gap in 1829. The row was finally connected in 1846.

Lafayette's cornerstone is still in that wall. It was reset there during the remodeling of 1882.

pins.title: Waterfront Park
pins.tease: Eighty-three oil tanks used to stand where you are standing
pins.stand_at: Stand on the promenade in the middle of Waterfront Park, on the lawn above the boardwalk, facing the lake.
pins.script:
You are standing on a lawn at the edge of a lake. Hold on to that, because for most of this city's history you could not have stood here, and you would not have wanted to.

In the eighteen hundreds this was one of the busiest lumberyards in the world. When the lumber companies needed more ground, they made it, filling the shallows out into the lake. Part of what is under your feet is manufactured land.

The Depression finished the lumber trade. By 1935 the failing yards had been replaced with fuel storage holding five and a half million gallons. And it grew. By 1958 there were eighty-three tanks on this waterfront holding eighty-four million gallons. Around them: rail sidings, junkyards, rusting equipment, a coal-burning power plant, and derelict boats rotting in the harbor.

Getting out of that took decades. In 1975 the city passed an ordinance giving the oil companies twenty years to leave. A 1982 poll found eighty-one percent of people here wanted public access to the water. In December of 1985, voters killed a bond that would have put condominiums, a seven story hotel and a parking garage on this ground.

Then the argument went to court. In 1989 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled that filled land on this lakefront is impressed by the public trust doctrine. It belongs to the public, and it can only be used for parks, recreation and things that actually need to be on the water. That decision let the city acquire more than sixty acres from the railroad. It also made the land cheap, because nobody could put condominiums on it anymore.

The community boathouse opened in 1988. This park, ten and a half acres of it, opened with its boardwalk in 1991.

The work did not stop there. In August of 2014 the city broke ground on the stretch north of here: a rebuilt bike path, environmental cleanup, power lines buried, and a public skate park. That package cost nine point one million dollars, and the ribbon was cut in November of 2015.
